records.title: Pocong: The Shrouded Shuffling Ghost of Cemeteries
records.summary: The most iconic and feared entity of Indonesian urban and rural ghostlore, the Pocong is an animated corpse wrapped in white Islamic burial shrouds (kain kafan). According to Muslim burial tradition in Indonesia, the shroud must be unknotted at the head, waist, and feet before interment; if the knots are left tied, the restless soul is trapped and rises from the grave after forty days to plead for release. With its feet bound tightly in cloth, the Pocong cannot walk, instead rolling, hopping, or floating silently through cemeteries and banana groves. Its pale, rotting face and dark empty eye sockets gaze at nocturnal travelers, causing terrifying paralysis.
records.historical_period: Traditional Islamic Syncretism to Contemporary Indonesian Horror Culture
records.region_or_community: Cemeteries and rural villages nationwide across Indonesia
geographic_associations: Cemeteries throughout Java, Sumatra, and Kalimantan

records.title: Kuntilanak: The Red-Eyed Maiden in the Banana Grove
records.summary: Feared across Indonesia and the wider Malay world (as Pontianak), the Kuntilanak is the vengeful female spirit (hantu) of a woman who died during childbirth. Manifesting as an exceptionally pale maiden in a long, bloodstained white dress with wild black hair cascading to her ankles, she conceals a deep gaping hole in the back of her neck or spine. Roosting in tall banyan, waru, or banana trees, her presence is heralded by the strong scent of sweet frangipani blossoms shifting suddenly to rotting carcasses, followed by a high-pitched, mocking laughter that sounds near when she is far and far when she is right beside you.
records.historical_period: Pre-Colonial animism through contemporary Indonesian urban cinema
records.region_or_community: Nationwide across Java, Sumatra, and Pontianak (West Kalimantan)

records.title: The Headless Pastor of Jeruk Purut Cemetery
records.summary: Located in Cilandak, South Jakarta, the historic Jeruk Purut Cemetery was established during the Dutch colonial era. The preeminent urban legend of Jakarta centers on the 'Pastor Kepala Buntung' (The Headless Pastor), a Dutch colonial Catholic priest who was decapitated by local bandits during colonial unrest. Nocturnal visitors and cemetery security guards report encountering the priest dressed in black cassock robes walking among the overgrown gravestones carrying his severed head beneath his arm, accompanied by a faithful, phantom black dog. Urban legend dictates that visitors can only summon him on Friday nights if they walk through the cemetery in odd-numbered groups.
records.historical_period: Colonial Dutch Era origin to Modern Jakarta Ghostlore

records.title: Tuyul: The Child Demon Coin-Stealer
records.summary: In Indonesian black magic (pesugihan) folklore, a Tuyul is a small, bald supernatural familiar resembling a naked toddler or pale green infant. Covetous human masters enter pacts with shamans (dukun) to acquire a Tuyul in order to become wealthy without working. The spirit sneaks into neighbors' bedrooms and commercial cash drawers through keyholes, invisibly siphoning small amounts of paper banknotes and coins. In exchange, the master's wife must breastfeed the demon blood from her chest. To foil a Tuyul, traditional Javanese households place bowls of green beans, crabs, or small mirrors near cash drawers, knowing the childish spirit will be distracted playing with beans or terrified by its own reflection.
records.historical_period: Pre-Colonial Javanese Animism to Modern Urban Economic Folklore
records.region_or_community: Urban and rural markets across Java and Sumatra

records.title: Wewe Gombel: The Child-Kidnapping Spirit of Semarang
records.summary: Rooted in the Gombel hills of Semarang, Central Java, Wewe Gombel is a maternal supernatural female phantom with wild tangled hair, long fangs, and colossal, pendulous sagging breasts. In local lore, she was an infertile woman driven to suicide after being abused and abandoned by her husband. Rather than harming children, Wewe Gombel kidnaps neglected, mistreated children who wander outside at dusk (maghrib), hiding them high in the branches of palm trees and feeding them human excrement disguised as delicacies. She cares for them affectionately until their negligent parents realize their wrongdoing and beat kitchen woks and pans through the village shouting her name, forcing her to return the child unharmed.
alternate_names: The Child Protector of Bukit Gombel
records.historical_period: Traditional Javanese rural lore to Contemporary Urban Legend

records.title: The Tragic Track 13 of the Bintaro Train Collision
records.summary: On October 19, 1987, Indonesia suffered its worst railway catastrophe when two passenger trains collided head-on near Pondok Betung in Bintaro, South Jakarta, resulting in 156 deaths and hundreds of severe mutilations. In Indonesian urban folklore, the railway tracks and the Manggarai train graveyard where the mangled steel carriages were stored became centers of terrifying paranormal encounters. Local residents and railway workers report seeing phantom passenger heads rolling along the rails at midnight, disembodied cries of victims trapped in twisted metal, and phantom trains roaring silently down Track 13 without headlights.
records.region_or_community: Bintaro, South Jakarta and Manggarai, Jakarta

records.title: Lawang Sewu: The Thousand Doors of Semarang
records.summary: Constructed in 1904 as the headquarters of the Dutch East Indies Railway Company (NIS) in Semarang, Central Java, Lawang Sewu ('Thousand Doors') is a colossal colonial building featuring hundreds of arched doors, stained-glass windows, and cavernous subterranean water-cooled basements. During World War II, the Japanese military converted the flooded basements into a brutal interrogation prison where Dutch and Indonesian prisoners were tortured and executed. Renowned as one of Asia's most haunted colonial buildings, visitors and night guards report apparitions of Dutch aristocratic ladies, headless prisoners in shackles, and the weeping spirit of a young Dutch maiden in the flooded tunnels.

records.title: Si Manis Jembatan Ancol: Sweet Maiden of Ancol Bridge
records.summary: A legendary staple of 20th-century Batavia and Jakarta urban folklore, Si Manis Jembatan Ancol ('The Sweet Maiden of Ancol Bridge') centers on Maryam (or Siti Ariah), a beautiful 19th-century Betawi maiden who fled the unwanted advances of a wealthy colonial merchant. Ambushed near the Ancol canal bridge in North Jakarta, she was murdered and thrown into the swampy waters. Beginning in the 1950s, nocturnal motorists and boatmen reported picking up an attractive young woman in a yellow kebaya who paid her fare in banana leaves or vanished after asking to cross the bridge. The legend was crystallized in modern Indonesian popular culture through iconic 1990s television adaptations.

records.title: Kolor Ijo: The Green Underwear Spectral Robber
records.summary: In 2003 and 2004 across Jakarta, West Java, and Banten, an acute moral and supernatural panic erupted regarding Kolor Ijo ('The Green Underwear Man'). According to widespread suburban rumors, a practitioner of dark black magic (ilmu hitam) was required to violate virgin maidens in forty different homes while wearing only a pair of enchanted green shorts (kolor ijo) and carrying an invisibility amulet to achieve absolute wealth and invulnerability. Terrified neighborhood watch patrols (ronda) armed with bamboo sticks and machetes kept round-the-clock vigils, placing garlic and kelor tree leaves on doorframes to repel the invisible intruder.
geographic_associations: Suburban residential districts of Bekasi, Tangerang, and Jakarta

records.title: The Ghost Ambulance of Bahureksa Street in Bandung
records.summary: Stationed for decades outside a grand Dutch colonial house on Jalan Bahureksa in Bandung, West Java, an antiquated vintage ambulance was the center of a famous Sundanese urban legend. Legend claimed that during a colonial-era traffic accident, a Dutch family perished while being transported in the ambulance. Whenever the vintage vehicle was towed to garages or junkyards across Bandung, it was inexplicably found parked back outside the Bahureksa residence the next morning. Neighbors reported the vehicle's engine starting spontaneously at midnight, with its emergency headlights flashing and sirens howling with no driver inside.
records.region_or_community: Jalan Bahureksa, Citarum, Bandung, West Java
